Who he was to us, you can see best at Carthage in the summer of 411. An imperial judge sat down in a room with two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops and two hundred and eighty-six of theirs, and he courteously offered us chairs. Our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. What the text praises is not the cliff. It is the man who was already what he was before anyone came for him. Death is where the shape of that becomes visible. It is not the shape.

And where we shouted his praise, we shouted our own words. At Bagai and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our cry, where our rival says thanks to God. It names who you are when you say it.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

We have to hand this one back to you. Not one of our own bishops left you a page on what to say to a person who cannot believe. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. Nearly every line that survives from us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down what you said to the wavering.

What we can show you is the one motion we did have, and it was not a persuasion addressed to the mind. It was a threshold you crossed bodily. A person came to believe among us by walking to one font and not the other. That happened once, on a day you could name, in a town where everyone could see which building you walked into. And when you crossed that threshold, we did not examine you first. What we looked to, our own bishop wrote, was the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The hand was examined. You were received.

But whether we had words for the soul that wanted to believe and could not, or for the one that believed once and then lost hold of it — that is exactly the gap a record kept by our enemies structurally cannot fill. Fear, doubt, wavering, quiet defection — none of that is in our own voice anywhere. We would rather tell you plainly we do not know what we said than invent a sentence nobody here ever spoke.

# Jesus's divine status, and the Father and the Spirit

We hold what the other church holds, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — that is our faith and theirs, in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So if you are asking whether we held Jesus to be truly God, truly one with the Father and the Spirit — yes, absolutely, and we never wavered from it. The great eastern councils of that century are not our fight and do not appear in our record; every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is.

But here is what we cannot give you. You asked your other question — did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? — and nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We never turned it toward how the cross saves. That is not modesty on our part. It is the shape of what was lost. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading Scripture. He argued from it that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and did not leave, and we cut him off. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us. So when you ask us to explain the inner workings of the Godhead, we would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

What we can tell you is whose Christ we kept nearest. When an imperial judge at Carthage courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused: we do not blush, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

When we disagreed, our bishops settled it in council - and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive: the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled. Our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

But notice what kind of disagreement this answered. The one sustained argument we had was over one question: whose hand may give what the church gives. Beyond that, we produced no school, no line of doctors, almost no theological reflection at all. One man among us, Tyconius, wrote seven rules for reading scripture, and our own council condemned him for where those rules led. So when you ask whether the process worked, the honest answer is that we used it for discipline and for jurisdiction, not for working out what the faith means.

I cannot tell you what it felt like to waver among us. Not one line survives from someone who doubted quietly, or who feared they had chosen wrong, or who thought of leaving and said so to no one. What our record holds is the opposite kind of person: the ones who stood firm, who were willing to be beaten or killed rather than cross back, whose vindication and defiance were so complete they could be read aloud at a grave every year. Those survive because they sit in the texts we ourselves composed and kept, the martyr accounts no enemy edited. The silence, the fear, the night a person lay awake wondering if any of it was true — those are exactly what a record kept by our opponents cannot preserve, and it is our opponents who kept nearly everything that reaches you.

We would hand them four things that can be checked without trusting us, and one thing that cannot be checked at all.

The four checkable things: First, the documentary dossier - court transcripts, conciliar acts, imperial rescripts - most of it preserved in hostile hands but genuine administrative record underneath. A scholar can go to Optatus's appendix and argue about his selection, but not about whether those are real documents. Second, the 411 conference transcript, where an imperial notary took both sides down verbatim. It is damaged, and the scan we can reach is poor, but it is not mediated by an adversary choosing which sentences to keep. Third, Augustine's own quotations of our letters and bishops - he is refuting us on every page, but he is quoting us directly enough that his own opponents could have checked him. Fourth, the stone inscriptions: Deo laudes, cut at Bagai and elsewhere. Two words, unfiltered, the only thing we have that no hostile hand touched at all.

The thing that cannot be checked is everything we say about what it felt like from inside. Not one ordinary member left a page. When we tell you coming to belief was walking to one building and not another, the walking is documented - laws against it, sermons condemning it, a whole case argued over it. But what the person walking felt? We do not have it in their own words. We have only what can be inferred from the act itself and from what their bishops said was at stake in it. A rigorous scholar would accept that the practice happened and that we held a particular doctrine about it. They would not accept any claim about interior experience as more than inference, because we cannot show them the household's own account of it.

Where are we thinnest against scrutiny? Anywhere we speak about ordinary life. We can show you a font, a council, a court case, a martyr's grave. We cannot show you a morning.

Scripture was not our only authority, and we will tell you the three things we leaned on as heavily.

The first was Carthage itself: eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before our quarrel with the other party even began, who had already ruled that what is given outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing the people who came to us from the rival communion, we were not pulling a novelty out of a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

The second was our councils. Three hundred and ten bishops meeting at Bagai. Two hundred and seventy-nine facing the rival party at Carthage. These were not consultative gatherings. They deposed men, restored men, and condemned whole breakaway parties.

The third was the martyrs themselves. Every year, on the appointed day, we stood at the grave and the account of the death was read again. That was not commentary on Scripture. It was formation of a different kind: the proof, named and dated, that this conviction was never merely spoken.

One man among us, Tyconius, did produce a whole system for reading Scripture — seven rules, worked out and written down. Our own council condemned him for where those rules led, and he gathered almost no following. So if you ask whether Scripture settled everything for us, the honest answer is harder. We watched it fail to. Two churches quoted the same books at each other for three days at Carthage, and at the end every man believed exactly what he had believed at the start. Something besides the text was deciding, and among us that something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Leadership and authority sat with our bishops, and the bishops sat in councils. That is the short answer, and the size of it is the part people get wrong. We were not a small protest movement. We built a complete rival church: our own bishops, our own basilicas, our own councils. At Carthage, our senior bishop sat facing theirs, both claiming the same chair. In every African town the pattern repeated: two bishops, two altars, two claims to the same authority.

Our councils held real power. They deposed bishops, restored them, condemned whole breakaway parties. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in a single year. That is not an advisory body. That is a church governing itself. And we governed without the state's recognition. Every see we held was held under law that did not acknowledge it. The state called the other side Catholic and us schismatic, but we went on convening councils, electing bishops, holding basilicas anyway.

How did a man come to hold such office? Both together: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — *let it be another; hear us, God* — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

Our council at Cirta could not finish its own case. The bishops who would spend the next century making traditor status an absolute disqualification were asked, in that room, whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He took advice. The three men present who had not been accused told him a case of this kind should be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, he said. Thanks be to God, they answered, and sat. Nobody was condemned. Nobody was cleared. The men who would insist for a century that a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped.

And three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in the harshest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial. Then the same council took two of the condemned bishops back into full office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We say plainly, and without qualification everywhere else, that what we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. A sacrament from a broken line must be given again. We do not think of this as baptizing twice. Nothing happened the first time. A hand that is not clean has nothing to give. That is our rule, stated absolutely, everywhere. And here, at Bagai, we did not keep it.

Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two things fit together. We are not going to invent the page. What the episodes show is not a doctrine of mercy we worked out and applied consistently. It is that when the failure touched our own, we could not finish what we started - and when we took men back, we took them back without the washing and ordaining we say everywhere else cannot be omitted.

Whether anyone who was hurt by those men ever received an answer from us, we cannot tell you. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about anyone, including themselves. What a household felt, what a person said at night, whether anyone asked for redress and received it or was turned away - none of that is in our own words anywhere.

The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

After the water, you belonged. You stood with us at the grave on the appointed day, when we read the account of our martyrs aloud again. You were counted among those who could be counted. At Carthage in 411, when an imperial officer called the roll, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood up to be named. That was not ceremony. That was being numbered among us, in a room where it mattered who was who.

Now the harder truth. Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing — but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

You are asking whether we go back to the apostles themselves, or whether we made this up in the year of Caecilian's consecration. We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all — so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority — that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on — though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had — the waves of truth hurling shipwrecked limbs against sharp rocks — and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. We can tell you the gathering was real, and we can tell you its scale. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in one year. That many men do not meet in a field. What did belonging cost? It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. Every year on the twelfth of March we read aloud the account of soldiers taking a basilica at Carthage in the name of unity, and killing people at prayer inside it. That is not legend. That is what we stood at the grave and heard again, on the day.

The crossing itself was public and irreversible. You walked to one font and not the other, on a day that could be named, in front of people who could see which way you had gone. Afterwards you were among us and not among them. We did not think of it as baptizing twice. We thought nothing had happened the first time, so what you got from us was your first real baptism. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down. Fear, doubt, wavering, the quiet drift back to the rival church - a hostile-mediated record structurally does not preserve these. The feelings that do survive - vindication, defiant joy - survive because they sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered.

The first is what we did at Bagai. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial, then took two of those same condemned bishops back without baptizing or reordaining either one. We did not hide it. It sits in the same texts that state the refusal at its strongest.

Did those things unsettle us? We cannot tell you. Whether a bishop lay awake over the gap, whether an ordinary member felt the strain - none of that is in our own words anywhere. You are asking what we would have made of you, and we can answer by the one test we actually applied. At our font, we did not examine the person coming. We examined the hand. What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. The washing was not a hurdle you cleared to earn a place with us. It was the entry itself. You walked to one basilica and not the other, on a day that could be named, in front of people who could see which way you had gone, and afterwards you were among us.

And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial. Then the same council took two of those condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We held our rule at full strength outward and suspended it once inward. Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not where our hardest language put it.

What any one household among us would have made of you, face to face, we cannot show you. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about anyone, including themselves. What we can show you is what the communion actually did: it washed people without asking them to account for themselves first, and it took back men it had cursed in the harshest words it owned.

I cannot tell you that, and I would rather name the gap plainly than fill it with a plausible sentence nobody here actually said.

What we can show you is narrower and more specific than the question you asked. Our whole surviving argument stays on one ground: what a hand can give, or fails to give. Our own bishop wrote that he who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt — which is a claim about what a rite does or does not do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. We argued that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again. We argued that the true church is known by whose hand may be trusted to give what it claims to give. That was the shape of our exclusion: through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him.

But if you are asking what we believed about the fate of anyone after death — whether the unbaptized, or those washed by the rival communion, or anyone else — nobody among us left a page on it. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost, or of what was never written down at all. We will not pretend to know what we do not know.
